title: Caste in Indian Politics

cards.h: Caste is central to Paper I Section B
cards.b:
Caste and politics is asked almost every year. The question is rarely "what is caste?" It is "how do caste and democracy shape each other?"

Two slogans help. Rajni Kothari said: it is not casteism in politics but the politicisation of caste. Politicians use caste to organise votes, but in doing so they also change caste itself, as groups form associations, make alliances and demand shares of power.

M.N. Srinivas (the dominant caste), the Rudolphs (caste associations), Kothari (politicisation) and Jaffrelot (the OBC rise) are the core names. Add the legal story: reservation, the Mandal Commission, Indra Sawhney (1992), the EWS quota (2019) and SC sub-classification (2024).

The latest chapter is the decision to include caste in Census 2027.

cards.h: Four scholars on caste and politics
cards.b:
M.N. Srinivas

In Religion and Society among the Coorgs of South India (1952) he gave Sanskritisation: lower castes imitate the customs of upper castes to rise. In "The Dominant Caste in Rampura" (1959), and later essays, he defined the dominant caste: numerous, owning land and ritually respectable, such as Vokkaligas, Jats, Patidars and Yadavs. They dominate local politics.

Rajni Kothari, Caste in Indian Politics (1970)

Caste is a resource and a ladder in competitive politics. Politics draws caste into a secular role, so caste becomes more about interest than ritual rank.

Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph, The Modernity of Tradition (1967)

Caste associations make traditional loyalty a tool for democracy. They also described three modes of political mobilisation: vertical, horizontal and differential.

Louis Dumont, Homo Hierarchicus (1966)

Caste is a system of ritual hierarchy based on purity and pollution. Critics say his model ignores power and politics.

cards.h: Ambedkar, Phule and the Dalit challenge
cards.b:
Jotirao Phule (Gulamgiri, 1873) attacked Brahminical domination. Periyar E.V. Ramasamy led the Self-Respect Movement from 1925.

B.R. Ambedkar is central. In Annihilation of Caste (1936), he argued that caste is not just division of labour but a division of labourers, and that it cannot be reformed without destroying the authority of the shastras. In Castes in India (1916) he called it an "enclosed class" shaped by endogamy. He demanded separate electorates; the Poona Pact (1932) with Gandhi gave reserved seats within general electorates instead.

The Constitution abolished untouchability (Article 17) and allowed reservation. After 1956, Ambedkar's followers built political groups, from the Republican Party of India to the Dalit Panthers (Maharashtra, 1972) and the BSP (1984, Kanshi Ram), which pushed bahujan unity.

• Article 15(4), 16(4): special provisions and reservation in jobs for backward classes. 15(5) (93rd Amendment, 2005): reservation in educational institutions, including private unaided ones.
  • Article 17: untouchability abolished. Laws: Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955; SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.
  • Articles 330 and 332: reserved seats for SC and ST in the Lok Sabha and Assemblies; 243D, 243T: in local bodies.
  • Article 335: claims of SC/ST in services consistent with administration efficiency.
  • Article 340: commission on backward classes. 102nd Amendment (2018): National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) given constitutional status (Article 338B).
  • Articles 341 and 342: President lists Scheduled Castes and Tribes.
  • 103rd Amendment (2019): 10% reservation for the economically weaker sections (EWS) among those not covered by existing quotas (Articles 15(6), 16(6)).

• Kaka Kalelkar Commission (1953-55): first Backward Classes Commission; not acted upon.
  • Mandal Commission (set up 1979 under B.P. Mandal; report 1980): OBCs about 52% of the population; recommended 27% reservation so the total stays under 50%. V.P. Singh announced implementation on 7 August 1990. This led to protests and the rise of OBC politics.
  • Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (16 November 1992, nine judges): upheld 27% for OBCs; creamy layer excluded; 50% ceiling (with narrow exceptions); no reservation in promotion. Parliament overrode the last through the 77th Amendment (1995), adding Article 16(4A).

cards.h: Phases of caste in electoral politics
cards.b:
1. Congress era: upper castes, Dalits and Muslims in a "catch-all" coalition. In Gujarat, Madhavsinh Solanki's KHAM strategy (1980s) combined Kshatriyas, Harijans, Adivasis and Muslims.
  2. Backward-caste upsurge (from 1967, strong after 1990): Lohia's socialist call for 60% preference for backward groups; Charan Singh's peasant base; Mandal brought SP, RJD, JD(U).
  3. Dalit assertion: BSP won power in Uttar Pradesh four times, with Mayawati as Chief Minister.
  4. Fragmentation and sub-castes: the BJP's "social engineering" courts non-dominant OBCs and non-Jatav Dalits; Nitish Kumar built a base of Most Backward and extremely backward groups.
  5. Welfare plus identity: parties now mix caste, religion and benefits.

Jaffrelot called the rise of lower castes into power a "silent revolution". Critics say it has benefited dominant sub-castes more than the most disadvantaged.

• EWS quota: upheld 3-2 in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (7 November 2022).
  • Maratha quota: the Court struck down the 2018 law in Jaishri Patil (May 2021) for breaching the 50% cap. The 102nd Amendment was read to remove state power to list OBCs; the 105th Amendment (2021) restored it. Maharashtra passed a fresh 10% Maratha law in February 2024.
  • Sub-classification: in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (1 August 2024), a seven-judge bench (6:1) overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004) and said states may sub-classify Scheduled Castes if based on data on inadequate representation. Some judges urged a creamy layer for SCs and STs; the Union Cabinet said it would not apply it.
  • Bihar: the 2023 caste survey found OBCs and EBCs near 63% of the population; the state raised quotas to 65%, but the Patna High Court struck this down in June 2024.
  • OBC sub-categorisation: the Rohini Commission (2017, report 2023).
  • Caste in the census: the Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs approved this on 30 April 2025. Census 2027's population phase (February 2027) includes a caste question; the last full count was in 1931.

Caste is declining: Dipankar Gupta, in Interrogating Caste (2000), argued that hierarchy has weakened and caste today is "difference", not rank. Urbanisation, education and market jobs reduce ritual hierarchy.

Caste is persisting or being reinvented:

  • Atrocities continue (Khairlanji 2006, Una 2016, Hathras 2020).
  • Marriage remains largely within caste; surveys show little inter-caste marriage.
  • Nicholas Dirks, Castes of Mind (2001), argued colonial census and law hardened caste identities. The 2027 count may do so again.
  • Class cuts across caste: a growing "creamy layer" benefits from quotas, and poor upper castes feel left out (the EWS argument).

A strong answer says caste has changed from ritual rank to political and economic identity, but remains a resource and a source of exclusion.

• Caste census: 30 April 2025 decision and the 2027 count could reshape reservation debates and constituency politics; opposition parties argue for removal of the 50% ceiling.
  • State surveys: Bihar (2023), Karnataka and Telangana (2025) held their own surveys, which the Union argued should be done by census alone.
  • Davinder Singh: the SC sub-quota debate in Punjab, Haryana and Telangana.
  • Atrocities Act: after the Supreme Court diluted arrest rules in 2018, protests led Parliament to restore them by amendment (2018).
  • Maratha, Patidar, Jat, Kapu groups: dominant castes seeking OBC status.
  • Panchayats: reserved seats shape village politics.

"Caste is both a source of exclusion and a resource for political mobilisation." Discuss.
"Examine the impact of the Mandal Commission on Indian politics."
"Has the reservation policy achieved its objectives? Examine the issues of creamy layer and sub-classification."
"Explain Srinivas's Sanskritisation and the dominant caste."

Structure: Kothari's "politicisation of caste"; scholars (Srinivas, Rudolphs, Dumont, Ambedkar, Jaffrelot); constitutional provisions; Mandal and Indra Sawhney; EWS and Davinder Singh; political phases (Congress, Mandal, BSP, BJP engineering); critique (Gupta vs Dirks); end with the 2027 census as the next turning point.
